narrative:
Your application was denied because the model estimated a 96% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That is a very high risk estimate, so the school treated admission as too risky, even though this is a prediction rather than a certainty.

In order of influence, your third-year class-rank decile was the strongest factor pushing toward predicted failure: you were in the lowest decile (1.00), while accepted students averaged around 5.79. Your LSAT score was the next strongest factor: 24 is well below the accepted-student average of about 37.18, and it also pushed toward failure. Your first-year class-rank decile reinforced that pattern: you were again in the lowest decile (1.00 versus an accepted average near 6.00). These academic indicators, especially your later-year standing and LSAT, drove the denial. Your gender and race were not used in the prediction.

To improve future chances, ask admissions for feedback or appeal options. Consider retaking the LSAT with structured preparation, strengthening your academic record through rigorous analytical or legal-writing coursework, and documenting a realistic bar-exam study plan. You could also ask whether conditional admission, delayed entry, or waitlist reconsideration after demonstrated improvement is possible.
